Subject: Multi-site control plane collocation & egress strategy — initial ask

Hi Karthik,

Thanks again for the demos last week. We're starting the internal architecture review for an EdgeBridge private deployment (3 sites: Amsterdam, Dublin, Frankfurt) and want Redwood's guidance on two questions that will materially affect our network design and procurement:

1) Control plane placement: we can either collocate the control plane on each site (smaller, independent control plane instances per site) or run a centralized control plane in a single region with data plane nodes at each colo. Pros/cons from a performance, operational, and compliance perspective would be helpful.

2) Egress strategy: we have strict egress auditing needs and want to understand recommended patterns for NAT/eProxy placement, BGP flows, and how to minimize cross-site egress charges while satisfying audit/logging/SOC expectations.

I've attached our current network diagrams and a short spreadsheet with traffic estimates. A few other constraints: we must integrate with our on-prem KMS (Thales HSM via KMIP), customer audit logs must include per-request model and token accounting, and our security team prefers minimal central egress to avoid international data transfers.

Can you run this by your architecture team and propose a short readout (1–2 pages) plus an annotated diagram showing recommended control/data plane topology and egress placement? We're targeting a decision by May 20 to progress crossconnects.

Attaching: edgebridge_multi_site_diagrams_v2.pdf, cp-dataplane-collocation-comparison.xlsx

Best,
Sara
VP Product
EdgeBridge Inc.

Subject: Re: Multi-site control plane collocation & egress strategy — initial ask

Sara / team,

Thanks — this is a great brief. Short summary up front: for your constraints (EU-only data residency preference, per-request audit, HSM/KMIP integration) my recommendation is regional control planes (one per major metro) with a lightweight central management plane for policy/config orchestration. Rationale and tradeoffs below.

High-level recommendation (one line): deploy small control plane instances co-located with data plane in each colo (Amsterdam, Dublin, Frankfurt), with a central policy/control coordinator in a single EU region for rollout coordination and analytics.

Why this pattern?
- Latency & availability: collocating control plane reduces control-loop latency for placements and cache warmups, and avoids cross-site control chatter during failover.
- Compliance: local control planes keep control-plane metadata and audit trails within site boundaries if you choose that config; central coordinator can be configured only to carry minimal metadata (policy blobs, not request tokens).
- Cost & egress: per-site control plane avoids cross-site control traffic egress, but you still need a central egress pattern for telemetry and long-term metrics (we recommend batching and an aggregated telemetry collector to minimize charges).

Key design points / checklist:
1) KMS/HSM: integrate via customer-provided KMIP gateway in each site. Control plane instances should be able to call KMIP endpoints locally; avoid proxying keys through central coordinator.
2) Audit & token accounting: enable token-level logging at the ingress edge (sidecar or egress proxy) and stream logs to your internal SIEM via a local aggregator. Redwood's runtime can emit per-request model_id, model_version, token_count fields — ensure the aggregator preserves these fields for SOC evidence.
3) Egress topology options (favored):
   - Local egress with mirrored telemetry: data egress (model downloads, container images) should be local where possible; outbound request flows to external services should be NAT'd at each site.
   - Centralized telemetry/durable storage: metrics + long-term traces can be sent to a central EU analytics cluster over an authenticated, compressed channel; use batching window to reduce tokens and bandwidth.
4) BGP & routing: prefer local BGP peerings for each site to reduce cross-site hairpin. If you need an active/standby path to a central collector, use policy-based routing and prefix-lists to avoid accidentally routing production inference egress through the central path.

Open questions / blockers I want Jordan to validate:
- BGP community tags you can set for preference across interconnects (Jordan, can you confirm current EdgeBridge colo community plan?)
- NAT pool sizing for concurrent inference streams (we estimated 1.2M concurrent ephemeral sessions at peak)
- SIEM ingestion SLA and whether you can accept batched telemetry (Jim from DataConnector may have an implementation note)

Action items:
- Jordan: review attached diagrams and add BGP/nat snippets (JIRA INF-9321).
- Kimberly: once Jordan confirms, we’ll produce a 2-page readout and a single-page annotated diagram for your security sign-off.

I'll attach a quick sketch and a comparison sheet I made.

Thanks,
Karthik

Karthik / Sara,

Attaching: annotated-bgp-snippets.txt (small config snippets), edgebridge_multi_site_diagrams_v2_annotated.pdf

Quick callouts:
- BGP community plan: I recommend using communities 65000:10/20 per-primary/per-secondary to steer egress to local providers. I've included sample route-maps for Juniper/Arista.
- NAT sizing: based on your peak numbers, use a 1:1 mapping for ephemeral NAT entries and reserve a 25% headroom. If you want to avoid large NAT tables on border routers, push ephemeral outbound through a local egress proxy cluster (containerized) with connection pooling.
- Egress auditing: put a lightweight TLS-terminating proxy cluster at each site that stamps a per-request UUID and forwards logs to your SIEM. That avoids coupling control plane tokens to telemetry streams.

I've included line comments on pages 2 and 3 where I think you should change the HA pairings for control plane nodes (move one control replica into an adjacent metro rather than colocating all three replicas in separate racks).

Jordan Blake
Senior Network Architect
Redwood Inference
